candidate_relations.reason: The record reports prior transient liver-enzyme elevation on statins but no current liver disease capable of explaining the persistent direct-versus-calculated LDL discordance.
ApoB was measured during investigation, but the referenced explanation is excess lipoprotein(a), not an ApoB-specific dyslipidemia.
Hip pain and elevated liver enzymes occurred during previous statin trials, but that intolerance does not cause the marked difference between direct and calculated LDL-C.
No ApoB mutation or defining ApoB abnormality is supplied, whereas the diagnostic object attributes the assay discordance to lipoprotein(a).
Lp(a) hyperlipoproteinemia captures the causal lipid abnormality under investigation, but omits the resulting discordance between direct and calculated LDL-C.
The case's target explanation is elevated Lp(a), so assigning the lipid discrepancy to an ApoB abnormality changes the specified cause.
Prior hip pain on several statins is clinically relevant intolerance, but it is separate from the LDL measurement discordance observed off and on therapy.
The record emphasizes disagreement between two LDL-C methods rather than documented simultaneous elevation of triglycerides and LDL-C required for mixed hyperlipidemia.
Serial direct LDL-C values near 113–115 mg/dL versus a calculated value of 170 mg/dL document the discrepancy, but the label omits elevated Lp(a) as its cause.
Type 2 diabetes is part of the history but does not by itself explain why direct and calculated LDL-C measurements diverged markedly.
Hypertension, diabetes, and high LDL create cardiovascular risk, but no atherosclerotic event is the diagnostic explanation for the laboratory discordance.
No juvenile cataracts, tendon xanthomas, neurologic disease, or cholestanol testing suggests cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis.
An untreated LDL-C of 232 mg/dL is incompatible with ApoB deficiency, which produces very low ApoB-containing lipoproteins.
Apart from medication-associated enzyme elevations, there is no current hepatic diagnosis or abnormal examination offered to account for the lipid findings.
The history of statin-associated hip pain is distinct from the later laboratory phenomenon involving calculated and direct LDL-C.
Lipoprotein(a) hyperlipoproteinemia identifies the stated cause, but the complete reference also requires its effect on direct versus calculated LDL cholesterol.
The adult has no xanthomas, premature vascular presentation, hematologic abnormalities, or phytosterol measurements supporting sitosterolemia.
The two LDL methods disagree, but calling this an LDL-C measurement disorder substitutes an assay defect for the specified biological interference from elevated Lp(a).
